How long will a Jackery Explorer 1000 Plus run a home oxygen concentrator? (US 120 V)

Tight fit 3.0 h

It is the start, not the running — except that no start-up figure reaches this comparison from either side, so there was nothing to compare. A missing figure is not read here as a pass: with no inrush to check against a ceiling, the verdict is held short of a clear yes rather than granted one. Running draw is 310 W, and the watts are settled; it is the start that is not.

Derived from official coefficients + Derived by WattPair · verified 2026-08-09 · US 120 V unit × home oxygen concentrator

Usable capacity 1,011.7 Wh
Surge headroom —

Running310 Wof2,000 Wcontinuous output

0 – 2,000 W across the rails above

No start-up rail: a start-up figure for this load.

Two numbers decide this, and readers use them interchangeably: watts are the ceiling on what the inverter holds at any instant, watt-hours are how much energy the battery holds. A machine can have plenty of one and not enough of the other.

The verdict is a calculation, not a lookup; the hours are a division, not the nameplate watt-hours. The working is in the evidence below.

This page answers an electrical question, not a medical one.

Where this page puts hours on a pairing, that figure is how long a power station’s battery lasts running this machine’s wattage — an electricity calculation, not a judgment about whether a break in therapy is safe. It describes the battery and the machine, not a person’s health. Where a row shows an energy rate instead of hours, that is because we hold nothing for that build which would make a usable-capacity figure defensible.

Where a verdict below reads a tight fit — the amber triangle on a row in the list of stations — read it as don’t rely on this pairing, not as a compromise likely to hold anyway. Most of the verdicts below land there, and the reason is set out above; that state means the same thing here however it was arrived at — this site cannot clear the pairing with confidence, and that isn’t a passing grade with a footnote. Where a row says a check could not be run at all, that is a weaker claim than a near miss, not a stronger one.

What to do about a power interruption for this machine is a question for a clinician, the durable medical equipment (DME) supplier who set it up, or the manufacturer’s own guidance for it — not for this site. For the electricity side of an outage plan, this page can help: what a station needs to run this machine at all, and — where the figures exist to work it out — how long a given battery keeps it running.

Questions people ask about this pairing

Will a Jackery Explorer 1000 Plus run a home oxygen concentrator?
Yes, but with very little room. 310 W of running draw against 2,000 W of continuous output — 16% of it. Anything past 82% of continuous output drops out of the green on this site, because a rating is a ceiling and a hot afternoon is not a laboratory. The verdict is computed from running watts, and inverter waveform — the working is in the evidence section above.
How long will a Jackery Explorer 1000 Plus run a home oxygen concentrator?
About 3.0 hours on a full charge. That divides a usable-capacity figure derived from Jackery's own published usable-capacity coefficient by this load's duty-weighted draw plus the machine's own 22 W idle draw — not the nameplate watt-hours divided by a label wattage, which is where the confident-looking 20–35% overstatements come from.
